newsitem.title: GERMANY: Deutsche Telekom offers returns despite big debts.
newsitem.headline: Deutsche Telekom offers returns despite big debts.

text.p: When the huge Deutsche Telekom flotation kicks off next week, the newly-privatised German telecommunications monopoly will take a leading place among a host of other privatised European telecoms stocks.

But size isn't everything, and many investors will be looking beyond the sheer scale of Telekom to see if the share will provide healthy rates of return on their investment compared to other European telecoms stocks.

Comparisons with other European telecoms companies, using a combination of Reuters Securities 3000 and analysts' reports, show that Deutsche Telekom rates quite highly in terms of profitability, but its performance is hindered by its debt.

BZW Bank in Frankfurt, in its recent report on Deutsche Telekom, said: "The most striking features of the Deutsche Telekom balance sheet are the absolute level of debt and the very high gearing levels."
BZW puts Deutsche Telekom just ahead of Turkey as the world's 25th-biggest debtor.

Deutsche Telekom's net debt of $67.64 billion dwarfs that of its nearest European competitor, British Telecom with $3.32 billion net debt. Its closest rival in the debt stakes is France Telecom, with $16.63 billion debt.

On the other hand, Telekom has the highest cash-flow of any of the world-wide telecoms companies, with $22 billion of EBITDA (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation) in 1995, the BZW report says.

From the investment side, BZW says Deutsche Telekom's return on equity, which expresses earnings as a percentage of equity capital and reserves to show how efficiently they are used, was 23.9 percent in 1995.

Although Deutsche Telekom comes relatively late to the privatisation game, its return on equity compares favourably with British Telecom Plc, which kicked off the privatisation trend in 1984 and is Europe's largest privatised telecoms company.
BT's return on equity comes out at 16.97 percent, followed by Tele Danmark, 49 percent of which was sold off by the Danish government in 1994, with 14.1 percent, according to Reuters Securities 3000.
Return on equity at the privatised Dutch telecoms group Koninklijke PTT Nederland (KPN) comes out at 15.45 percent.

"Based on an offering price of 30 marks, Telekom does not appear very attractive on either a price/earnings ratio or net dividend yield basis. However, the company does compare favourably when measured against peers on a price/cash flow basis," said Bank Julius Baer in its recent report on Telekom.
Julius Baer's estimates a current market price/earnings ratio of 14.5 for Deutsche Telekom, below that of KPN at 15.6 and BT at 15.8.

In terms of scale, BT is closest to Telekom in size. The recent merger of BT and the U.S. group MCI will create the world's fourth-biggest telecoms company based on combined sales in 1995 of $37.83 billion.
Deutsche Telekom's sales of $42.66 billion in 1995 put it in third place after Japan's NTT, AT&T in the U.S.
While sales give a good indicator of the sheer size of Telekom, the margin on sales is of more interest to the investor.

Bank Julius Baer says that Deutsche Telekom's operating margin in 1995 was 26.7 percent, a favourable rating for the company, while BZW estimates Deutsche Telekom's operating margin for 1995 at 27.8 percent.

Spain's Telefonica de Espana has the highest operating margin among the European telecoms stocks at 29.29 percent, followed by BT with 21.45 percent, Tele Danmark at 20.65 percent and Stet at 19.29 percent, Securities 3000 showed.
Despite its huge debt burden, analysts are mainly positive on the outlook for the Deutsche Telekom share.
"The (Telekom) board has made it clear that debt reduction takes precedence over investment in other markets," Deutsche Morgan Grenfell says in its report on the company.
"The company is equipped with a range of unique strengths, with which it should be able to reach its targets," DMG says.
